stem:
An awake adult on a NSW ward has a new nasogastric tube inserted for feeding; insertion was uneventful, with no coughing or distress. The aspirate, tested on a graded pH strip, reads 4.5. She takes a proton-pump inhibitor, and the nurse asks whether a chest x-ray is needed before use because acid suppression makes pH testing unreliable.

What should the medical officer advise?

options.label: A
options.text: Order a chest x-ray, as the PPI makes the pH unreliable
options.explanation: Acid suppression can raise gastric pH, so a correctly placed tube may fail the test and need an x-ray. It cannot make a respiratory aspirate acidic, so a pH of 5 or below still confirms gastric placement.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm with air insufflation and listening over the stomach
options.explanation: The air insufflation ('whoosh') test cannot distinguish gastric from respiratory or oesophageal placement and must not be used.

options.label: C
options.text: Document the pH and use the tube; no x-ray is needed
options.explanation: Under NSW guidance an aspirate pH of 5 or below on a graded strip confirms gastric placement on insertion. Document the pH and external length and use the tube; an x-ray is needed when the pH is above 5, no aspirate is obtained or there is clinical concern.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a carbon dioxide detector before allowing any feed
options.explanation: A carbon dioxide detector can suggest airway placement, but it is not the confirmation standard and adds nothing once a confirmatory pH has been obtained.

options.label: E
options.text: Repeat the pH in four hours before giving anything
options.explanation: Placement has already been confirmed. Waiting adds delay without improving safety; recheck before each use and if the tube may have moved.

context: Acid suppression can make a correctly placed tube fail the pH test, but a pH of 5 or below still confirms gastric placement; x-ray is for pH above 5, no aspirate or clinical concern.
